items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: He played Basie and Cab Calloway and Ellington and Fletcher Henderson.

ctx.x: And yeah, it’s an interesting ride. The whole thing that got me into this, along with the music, because I’m not old enough to have been there when it was really happening. I might have been on the planet in the 1950s, but I wasn’t making any clubs. But I was a fan of this music, I still am a fan of the music. I got lucky and took some guitar lessons as a very young kid and my instructors were jazz aficionados, jazz players. So my father played classical music around the house. items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Billy Mitchell from the Basie band?

ctx.x: But I wonder if your attitude about the music would have been different.

I wouldn’t have known half of the stuff that I found out the best way, from experience. The experience is the best teacher. The tuition is very high. Yeah. But it’s worth it ‘cause if they pluck you out of a music school, you might know how to play or execute, and then they make you leader. Well you don’t even know how to be a sideman. How can you be a leader if you’ve never been a sideman? And if you’ve never worked for a good leader and a bad leader, how do you know what it is to be a good leader? If you’ve…

Well how the heck does a student these days learn that protocol? You had sort of mentioned that in today’s jazz education it seems that there are some people are now teaching who weren’t able to participate in that learning process. So you have mostly book-schooled professors now teaching another generation.
